summary: A settled signature verdict no longer keeps a judging row. The rows earlier releases kept are deleted after upgrade, in short paced pages. Receipts from before 2026-10-07, which were kept for a deployment+30d follow-up, now expire through the ordinary response cleanup and its checks. Free pages go back 128 per write instead of 512, which keeps each write under 100 ms, and the hourly retention pass gives the freed pages back. Measured on a copy of a real member, this gave back 7.9% of the file (1.18 million of 14.9 million pages), about 1.5 KB per signed claim.

replay.detail: No graph replay and no history scan at open. Once the signature migration is done, the prune walks claim_signature_judging in claim order from a cursor in meta. Each writer loan covers 512 rows or 10 ms, followed by an equal quiet interval. Response cleanup keeps its 64-row, 20 ms chunks.

schema.detail: One trigger is added, claim_verdict_queue_marks_pruned. When a claim with no judging row is queued for judgment again, it gets a dirty placeholder row, so it reads as pending until rejudged, as a dirty row made it read before. One meta key is added: claim_signature_judging_prune, the prune cursor. No table, column, index, kind, digest or storage version changes; storage stays at 20.

rules.detail: Verdicts, signatures, nonces, candidates, the served per-claim signature (claim_signatures), dependency links (text or interned) and their requeue are unchanged. A row is deleted only when its fold is complete, clean, unblocked and notified, with at most 32 candidates matching claim_signature_counts. Such a claim is judged directly from its candidates and never reads the row. Claims with more than 32 candidates keep their completed result witness. Response retention stays 7 days. A legacy receipt below meta.idempotency_legacy_rowid has no recorded completion time, so cleanup treats it as due. It goes only when its effect is durably recognized, and a late retry then gets idempotency-key-expired with the original claim id. Otherwise it is kept, as any receipt without a durable identity is.

compatibility.detail: No synced table or digest changes, so peers of any version are unaffected in both directions (measured: replication inventory digest equal before and after the prune). The previous release reads a missing judging row as never paged: verdict reads see nothing pending, and its next judgment of the claim inserts a fresh row. It keeps the new queue trigger, which it does not know, so a revocation, nonce or root requeue it runs after a rollback still marks pruned claims pending. The client contract (docs/st3/client-v0) now says legacy receipts expire; nothing else in it changes.

downtime.detail: No downtime. Measured on a copy of the member: the prune took about 6,260 loans, longest 59 ms (p99 32 ms). Free pages went back at 128 per write: p50 18 ms, p99 52 ms. Across two runs, 1 of 19,629 writes exceeded 100 ms (113 ms), while the live daemon was writing to the same disk. At 64 pages per write the tail did not shrink (4 of 18,433 writes over 100 ms, up to 134 ms); at the earlier 512 it reached 225 ms. The daemon sleeps 50 ms between writes. Response cleanup keeps its 64-row, 20 ms chunks. In an earlier run of the same chunks over 141,000 receipts, its longest loan was 55 ms.

manual.detail: Nothing to do on a store with incremental auto-vacuum (PRAGMA auto_vacuum answers 2, as every store created from 2026-10-18 on does). A store created before then reuses the freed pages for new data but its file does not shrink. Convert it once with the daemon stopped, with free disk as large as the store, using the command in docs/st3/retention.md: python3 -c 'import sqlite3, sys; c = sqlite3.connect(sys.argv[1]); c.execute("PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL"); c.execute("VACUUM")' "$STATE/claims.sqlite3". It cannot be paced: a VACUUM rewrites the whole file in one write, so the daemon cannot run it.

recovery.detail: Rolling back to the previous release is supported. Deleted judging rows are resume state only: they are recomputed from the retained candidates whenever a claim is judged again. Expired legacy responses cannot be restored; their claims still identify the operation.
